verses.text: Paul came to Derbe and then to Lystra. A follower named Timothy lived there. His mother was a Jewish believer, but his father was a Greek.
The believers in Lystra and Iconium spoke well of him.
Paul wanted to take Timothy with him on the journey. So he circumcised him because of the Jews who lived in that area, since they all knew that his father was a Greek.
As they travelled from town to town, they gave the believers the rules decided by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, and told them to obey them.
So the churches were made stronger in the faith and grew in number every day.
Paul and his friends travelled through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, because the Holy Spirit had stopped them from preaching the word in Asia.
When they came to the border of Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus would not let them.
So they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas.
During the night Paul had a vision. A man from Macedonia was standing there, begging him, "Come over to Macedonia and help us."
After Paul had seen the vision, we got ready at once to leave for Macedonia. We were sure that God had called us to preach the good news to the people there.
From Troas we sailed straight to Samothrace, and the next day on to Neapolis.
From there we travelled to Philippi, a Roman colony and the leading city of that part of Macedonia. We stayed there several days.
On the Sabbath we went outside the city gate to the river, where we expected to find a place of prayer. We sat down and began to speak to the women who had gathered there.
One of those listening was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira. She sold expensive purple cloth, and she worshipped God. The Lord opened her heart to accept Paul's message.
She and the people of her house were baptised. Then she invited us to her home. "If you agree that I truly believe in the Lord," she said, "come and stay at my house." And she made us come.
One day, as we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit that told the future. She earned a lot of money for her owners by telling fortunes.
She followed Paul and the rest of us, shouting, "These men are servants of the Most High God. They are telling you the way to be saved."

She kept doing this for many days. Finally Paul became so troubled that he turned around and said to the spirit, "In the name of Jesus Christ I order you to come out of her!" At that very moment the spirit left her.
When her owners saw that their hope of making money was gone, they grabbed Paul and Silas and dragged them into the market place to face the authorities.
They brought them to the city officials and said, "These men are Jews, and they are making trouble in our city.
They are teaching customs that we Romans are not allowed to accept or practise."
The crowd joined the attack against Paul and Silas. The officials ordered them to be stripped and beaten with rods.
After they had been beaten many times, they were thrown into prison. The jailer was ordered to guard them carefully.
Because of this order, he put them in the inner cell and locked their feet between heavy blocks of wood.
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them.
Suddenly there was such a strong earthquake that the prison was shaken to its foundations. At once all the prison doors flew open, and everyone's chains came loose.
The jailer woke up, and when he saw the prison doors open, he pulled out his sword to kill himself. He thought the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul shouted, "Do not harm yourself! We are all here!"
The jailer called for lights, rushed in, and fell trembling before Paul and Silas.
Then he brought them out and asked, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?"
They answered, "Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household."
Then they told the word of the Lord to him and to everyone in his house.
At that hour of the night the jailer took them and washed their wounds. Then right away he and all his family were baptised.
He brought them into his house and gave them a meal. He and his whole family were filled with joy, because they had come to believe in God.
When it was daylight, the city officials sent their officers to the jailer with the order: "Let those men go."
The jailer told Paul, "The officials have ordered that you and Silas be set free. Now you can leave. Go in peace."

But Paul said to the officers, "They beat us in public without a trial, even though we are Roman citizens, and threw us into prison. And now they want to get rid of us secretly? No! Let them come themselves and lead us out."
The officers reported this to the city officials. When the officials heard that Paul and Silas were Roman citizens, they were afraid.
So they came and said they were sorry. They led them out of the prison and asked them to leave the city.
After Paul and Silas came out of the prison, they went to Lydia's house. There they met with the believers and encouraged them. Then they left.
